situational2.title: Situational writing · 6 more tasks with models

tasks.task:
Mr Devan, a veterinarian, gave a talk to your level about caring for pets. Your form teacher has asked you to write to him on behalf of the class.

Write an email to Mr Devan. You should include:
• what you are thanking him for
• one thing from the talk that your class found most useful
• what some pupils have done differently since the talk
• an invitation to a school event he might like to attend
tasks.pac: Purpose: to thank, and to invite. Audience: an adult visitor you do not know well — formal. Context: four bullet points. The second and third are where most pupils go thin; each needs one specific example, not a general compliment.
tasks.model:
To: devan@greenlanevet.com.sg
Subject: Thank you for your talk to our Primary 5 pupils

Dear Mr Devan,

I am writing on behalf of Primary 5 Integrity to thank you for the talk you gave us last Wednesday on caring for pets. You gave up an entire afternoon of your working week for us, and we are very grateful.

The part the class found most useful was your explanation of how to tell when an animal is in pain. Many of us had assumed that a hamster or a rabbit would cry out if something were wrong. Learning that small animals hide their pain, and that a change in eating or grooming is often the only sign, was new to almost everybody in the room.

Since the talk, several pupils have begun keeping a short weekly note of what their pet eats. One of my classmates noticed that her rabbit had stopped finishing its hay, took it to a clinic, and found that it had a tooth problem that was caught early. She asked me to tell you that.

Our school is holding its Green Fair on Saturday 18 July from nine in the morning until noon, and there will be a stall on responsible pet ownership run by our class. We would be delighted if you could come, although we understand that weekends may be busy for you.

Thank you once again for your time and your patience with our many questions.

Yours sincerely,
Nathan Wong
Primary 5 Integrity
Green Lane Primary School
tasks.why: All four points covered, and each one carries a specific detail rather than a general compliment. The third point is the strongest move in the whole answer: instead of saying "we all take better care of our pets now", it tells one small true-sounding story with an outcome. Formal register is held from the greeting to the sign-off — no contractions, no exclamation marks — and the invitation is polite without being pushy.

tasks.task:
Your friend Haziq is coming to your flat on Saturday for the first time to work on a group project. He has never been to your estate.

Write an email to Haziq. You should include:
• how to get to your block from the MRT station
• what time to come and how long you expect the work to take
• what he should bring
• what to do if he cannot find the place
tasks.pac: Purpose: to give directions and instructions. Audience: a friend — informal. Context: four bullet points. Directions must be in a sensible order, and the last point needs a real fallback, not "just call me".
tasks.model:
To: haziq.rahman@email.com
Subject: Getting to my place on Saturday

Hi Haziq,

Here's how to find my flat so you don't end up wandering around Yishun for half an hour.

Come out of Yishun MRT at Exit B, the one facing the bus interchange. Walk past the interchange and keep the big supermarket on your left. At the traffic light, cross over and you'll see three identical blocks — mine is the middle one, Block 726. The lift lobby is behind the bicycle racks, and I'm on the eleventh floor, unit 11-142. It's about eight minutes' walk in total.

Can you come at ten? I reckon we'll need about three hours for the model and the write-up, so we should be done by one. My mother says she'll feed us lunch, so don't eat before you come.

Bring your half of the research notes, a ruler and the glue gun if yours still works — mine gave up last week. I've already got the cardboard, the paint and the printer, so you don't need to worry about those.

If you get lost, call me on 9123 4567. If I don't pick up because I'm in the shower, wait at the mama shop next to the bicycle racks and I'll come down and find you — it's the only shop at the foot of my block, so you can't miss it.

See you Saturday!

Your friend,
Nathan
tasks.why: The directions run in the order the reader will walk them, with landmarks rather than street names, which is what actually helps. Informal tone throughout: contractions, a joke in the opening line, a question rather than an instruction about the time. The last point gives a genuine backup place to wait instead of the usual "just call me", which is what separates full task-fulfilment marks from partial ones.

tasks.task:
You are the class librarian. Your class ran a Reading Buddies scheme this term, in which Primary 6 pupils read with Primary 1 pupils every Friday. Your form teacher has asked for a report.

Write a report for your form teacher, Mrs Halim. You should include:
• how the scheme was run
• what went well
• one problem faced
• one recommendation for next term
tasks.pac: Purpose: to report. Audience: your form teacher — formal and factual. Context: a report, so use headings, no greeting, no chatty language, and no "I think it was fun".
tasks.model:
Report on the Primary 6 Reading Buddies Scheme
By: Nathan Wong, Class Librarian, Primary 6 Integrity
Date: 14 August 2026

Purpose
This report describes how the Reading Buddies scheme ran in Term 3 and recommends one change for Term 4.

How the scheme was run
Twenty-four Primary 6 pupils were each paired with one Primary 1 pupil. The pairs met in the school library every Friday from 1.30 p.m. to 2.15 p.m. over eight weeks. Each Primary 6 pupil chose two picture books a week from a shelf set aside by the librarian, read one aloud to the younger child, and then listened while the child attempted the second. A record card was signed after every session.

What went well
Attendance was high: 21 of the 24 pairs met in at least seven of the eight weeks. The younger pupils grew noticeably more willing to read aloud; nine of them read a whole book unaided by Week 8, compared with two in Week 1. Several Primary 6 pupils reported that having to explain words made them think harder about meanings themselves.

Problem faced
The library was too noisy. Twenty-four pairs reading aloud in one room meant that many pupils could not hear their partner and began to read more loudly, which made the problem worse. Three pairs moved into the corridor without asking, which was unsafe.

Recommendation
The scheme should be split into two groups of twelve pairs meeting on alternate Fridays, or the second group should be given the use of an empty classroom. Twelve pairs in the library would allow each pair to hear each other without raising their voices.
tasks.why: Report format handled properly: a title, the writer's role, a date, and four headings — no "Dear Mrs Halim" and no sign-off. The language is factual and the evidence is numerical, which is what a report is for. The problem is a real operational one with a named consequence, and the recommendation follows directly from it rather than being a general wish for improvement.

tasks.task:
Your school is collecting used story books for children at a nearby welfare home. You have been asked to write a notice to be put up on the noticeboard at every level.

Write a notice. You should include:
• what is being collected and who it is for
• what condition the books must be in
• where and when to bring them
• who to approach with questions
tasks.pac: Purpose: to inform and persuade. Audience: pupils across the whole school, including Primary 1 — semi-formal and very plain. Context: a notice, so use a heading, short lines, and no greeting or sign-off. A notice that a Primary 2 pupil cannot read has failed.
tasks.model:
BOOK DRIVE: GIVE A STORY A SECOND HOME

WHAT WE NEED
We are collecting used story books for the children at Sunrise Children's Home. They have a reading room with almost empty shelves. Picture books and easy chapter books are the most useful, because most of the children there are between five and ten years old.

WHAT WE CANNOT ACCEPT
Books must be clean, complete and readable. Please do not bring books with torn or missing pages, books that have been written in, or books that are damp. Textbooks and assessment books cannot be used.

WHERE AND WHEN
Bring your books to the two blue boxes outside the school library.
Collection runs from Monday 3 August to Friday 14 August, before school and during both recesses.
Please do not leave books on the floor if a box is full — tell the librarian instead.

QUESTIONS?
Speak to Nathan Wong of Primary 6 Integrity, or to Mrs Halim in the staff room.

One book from each of us fills a shelf. Thank you.
tasks.why: A notice has no greeting and no sign-off, and this one does not pretend to be a letter. Headings in capitals let a reader find one piece of information without reading the rest. The condition point is handled as a short "cannot accept" list, which is far clearer than a sentence, and the sentences stay short enough for a Primary 2 reader. The closing line persuades in seven words without slipping into an excitable tone.

tasks.task:
You borrowed a book from the public library and returned it three weeks late because it was left in your grandmother's flat in Malaysia during the holidays. You have been fined $6.30. You would like the library to reduce the fine.

Write an email to the library. You should include:
• the details of the book and the fine
• why the book was returned late
• what you have done about it
• what you are asking the library to do
tasks.pac: Purpose: to explain and to appeal. Audience: a library officer you do not know — formal, and *Dear Sir or Madam* with *Yours faithfully*. Context: an appeal must accept responsibility first. A response that blames the library or sounds as though the fine is unfair loses language marks even when all four points are covered.
tasks.model:
To: enquiries@nlb.gov.sg
Subject: Appeal regarding an overdue fine of $6.30 — member 30098

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am a Primary 6 pupil and a member of the Punggol Regional Library. I returned a book called *The Boy at the Back of the Class* on 12 June, three weeks after it was due, and I have been charged an overdue fine of $6.30.

The book was late because I took it with me to my grandmother's home in Johor Bahru during the school holidays and left it in her flat by mistake. We did not travel back until the first weekend of June, which was when I recovered it. I understand that this was my own carelessness and not the library's fault.

I returned the book on the same day that it came back into my hands, and it is undamaged. I have since written the due dates of my loans on the calendar in my kitchen so that this does not happen again, and I have paid $2.00 of the fine from my own pocket money.

I would be grateful if the library would consider reducing the remainder of the fine, as $6.30 is a large amount for me to pay out of my allowance. If that is not possible, I would like to ask whether I may pay the balance in instalments over the next two months. I will accept whichever decision you reach.

Thank you for taking the time to read my appeal.

Yours faithfully,
Nathan Wong
Member number 30098
tasks.why: The first line identifies the writer and the matter in one sentence, which is what a formal opening is for. Responsibility is accepted explicitly — "my own carelessness and not the library's fault" — and this is the move that makes an appeal work. The fourth point offers an alternative in case the request is refused, which shows a genuine grasp of audience. *Dear Sir or Madam* is correctly paired with *Yours faithfully*, and the reference number appears in the subject line where an officer needs it.

tasks.task:
You and your friend Priya were chosen for the school's badminton pair for the zonal finals. You have injured your wrist and the coach has replaced you. Priya does not know yet.

Write an email to Priya. You should include:
• what has happened
• how it happened and what the doctor said
• who will play with her instead, and what you think of that
• what you will do to support her
tasks.pac: Purpose: to tell a friend bad news kindly. Audience: a close friend — informal, but not flippant. Context: the difficulty here is tone. The news is disappointing for the reader too, so an email that is only about your own feelings has missed the audience.
tasks.model:
To: priya.s@email.com
Subject: Some bad news about the finals — read this before training

Hi Priya,

I wanted you to hear this from me before you heard it in the hall. I can't play in the zonal finals with you. Coach Tan told me this morning that he has to replace me.

It's my right wrist. I landed badly on it during the last set on Tuesday and it swelled up overnight. My mother took me to the clinic on Wednesday and the doctor said it's a sprain, not a break, but I have to keep the splint on for three weeks and I'm not allowed to hold a racket at all. The finals are in nine days, so there was no way around it. I did ask.

Coach has put Wei Ling in with you. I know she plays from further back than I do and you'll have to cover more of the net at first, but she has a much better smash than mine and she doesn't panic. Honestly, I think the two of you could go further than we would have. It took me until yesterday evening to be able to write that sentence and mean it.

I'll be at every training session, and I'll be the loudest person in the gallery on the day. If it helps, I can film your games so you and Wei Ling can watch them back — I've got nothing else to do with my hands for three weeks. And I still owe you a rematch once this splint comes off.

Don't let this throw you. You were the better half of that pair anyway.

Your friend,
Nathan
tasks.why: The subject line tells the reader why to open the message now, and the first sentence delivers the news without a paragraph of build-up. The third point does the hardest thing in the task: it says something generous about the replacement and admits how hard that was to write, which is both honest and kind. The support offered is concrete — filming the games — rather than "I'll support you". The tone stays informal through contractions and short sentences without becoming jokey about news the reader will find upsetting.

compositionP3b.title: Picture composition · 6 more four-picture tasks
compositionP3b.instruction: Four pictures tell a story. Write about 120 to 180 words. Use all four pictures, in order. Marks: 10 for content, 10 for language.
compositionP3b.helper:
1 BEGINNING — who, where, when
2 PROBLEM — what went wrong (pictures 2 and 3)
3 ENDING — how it was solved, and how you felt

tasks.model:
Last term, our teacher held a skipping trial to choose ten pupils for the Sports Day display. I wanted a place badly, but when my turn came my foot caught the rope on the fourth jump and I stumbled in front of the whole class. Two boys laughed.

That evening, I took my rope down to the corridor outside our flat and practised until it was dark. I did the same the next evening, and the next. Sometimes I managed forty jumps. Sometimes I tripped on the second one and sat down on the cold floor, wanting to give up.

I kept going because my grandmother said that a rope only obeys people who are stubborn.

On Sports Day, I skipped for two whole minutes without a single mistake. Mrs Kaur handed me a certificate and told me she had watched me practising from her window every evening. I was proud, but not of the certificate. I was proud of all the dark evenings nobody saw.
tasks.why: All four pictures are used in order, and the writer adds what the drawings cannot show: the term, the ten places, the two boys laughing, the grandmother's line about the rope. Past tense is held throughout. The ending does what a top-band P3 ending does — it names a feeling and then gives an unexpected reason for it, instead of stopping at "I was very happy".

tasks.model:
One Sunday morning, I was helping my father choose fish at the wet market when I heard a child crying somewhere behind the vegetable stalls. I went to look. A little boy of about four was standing alone between two crates, sobbing so hard that he could not speak.

I knelt down so that I was not taller than him and asked him his name. He said it was Ryan, and that he had let go of his mother's hand to look at a tank of crabs. He did not know his mother's phone number.

I took his hand and walked him to the information counter near the entrance. The uncle there made an announcement over the loudspeaker, and I stayed with Ryan and told him about my cat so that he would stop shaking.

Two minutes later, a woman came running down the aisle with her slippers slapping the wet floor. She lifted Ryan up and held him tightly for a long time.

She thanked me again and again. I only nodded, because my throat felt strange.
tasks.why: The story is told from a clear point of view with small, believable details the pictures do not contain — the crab tank, the slapping slippers, the cat used as a distraction. Notice the kneeling detail in the second paragraph: it shows kindness through an action rather than stating "I was very kind". The last line suggests emotion without naming it, which is a step beyond the usual "I felt very happy" ending.

tasks.model:
It rained so heavily on Tuesday afternoon that the drains outside our school were overflowing. I had brought my red umbrella, so I opened it and stepped out of the shelter feeling rather pleased with myself.

Then I saw Kamala standing at the gate. She was pressed against the railing with her bag held over her head, and her shoes were already soaked. She lived in the next block to mine, but we had never once walked home together because she was quiet and I had never bothered to speak to her.

I ran over and held the umbrella above both of us. It was not big enough for two, so my left shoulder was wet through by the time we reached our carpark. We talked the whole way. She was not quiet at all once somebody started.

The next morning, Kamala was waiting outside my classroom with a warm Milo from the canteen. We have eaten recess together every day since.

One wet shoulder, and I gained a friend I had walked past for two years.
tasks.why: The writer earns the last line by admitting something unflattering in the second paragraph — that she had never bothered to speak to Kamala. That admission is what turns a kind deed into a story. The soaked shoulder appears twice, first as a cost and then in the final sentence as a bargain, which gives the composition a shape. Past tense is consistent and the vocabulary is within reach of a Primary 3 writer: *overflowing, pressed, soaked, bothered*.

tasks.model:
In January, Mr Peh made me the plant monitor of Primary Four Diligence. He handed me a green watering can and told me that the chilli plant on our window ledge was now my responsibility. I promised I would look after it and I meant it.

Then came the long weekend. I spent three days playing games on my father's computer and never thought about the classroom once.

When I walked in on Tuesday morning, the plant had collapsed over the side of its pot. Its leaves were brown and curled, and one of them crumbled when I touched it. Nobody scolded me, which somehow made it worse. I sat at my desk and could not look at the window.

After that, I watered it every single morning before the bell. I moved the pot to the sunnier end of the ledge and pulled off the dead leaves. Six weeks later there were two small white flowers on it, and by June we had four chillies.

I learnt that a promise is not something you say. It is something you do every day, even on holidays.
tasks.why: The second paragraph is only two sentences long, and that is deliberate — the forgetting should feel quick and careless. "Nobody scolded me, which somehow made it worse" is the kind of honest line that moves content into the top band, because it shows guilt instead of announcing it. The recovery is specific: watering, moving the pot, pulling off dead leaves, a count of flowers and chillies. The closing lesson is stated in the writer's own words rather than as a borrowed proverb.

tasks.model:
My grandmother turned seventy in March. She had looked after my brother and me every afternoon since we were small, and we wanted to give her something she had not paid for herself.

For five weeks we saved every coin we were given, hiding the tin behind the rice cooker. When we counted it on the kitchen table, we had eighteen dollars and forty cents. It was enough for flour, eggs, butter and a packet of candles.

We baked the cake on Saturday while she was at the market. My brother wrote the card and I read the recipe aloud. Everything went well until we took the tin out of the oven. One side of the cake had risen and the other had not, so it leaned over like a tired old building. We stared at it in horror.

We frosted it anyway and hid the worst side against the wall of the plate.

When my grandmother came home and saw the candles, her eyes filled with tears. She said it was the best cake she had ever eaten, and she ate two slices to prove it.
tasks.why: The composition uses all four pictures but gives the third one the most space, because the lopsided cake is where the interest lies. Two details carry the whole story: the tin hidden behind the rice cooker, and hiding the worst side of the cake against the plate. The ending is moving without being sentimental, because the writer proves the claim — she ate two slices — rather than simply asserting that everybody was happy.

tasks.model:
I was the last runner in the Primary Four relay and my class had never won anything. When Bala slapped the baton into my hand we were second, only a few steps behind Primary Four Grace, and I thought we might finally do it.

Halfway down the straight, the girl in front of me caught her foot on the edge of the track and went down hard. Her baton bounced away and she did not get up.

I could have run past her. The finishing line was twenty metres away and nobody would have blamed me. Instead I stopped, pulled her up by the arm, and held on while she limped the rest of the way. Both our classes crossed the line last and second last, and the cheering stopped in a strange, sudden silence.

On Monday, Mr Raj called me out at assembly and gave me a Sportsmanship Award. The whole school clapped for a very long time.

I still do not have a medal for running. I have something on my wall that is harder to win.
tasks.why: "I could have run past her" is the strongest sentence in the composition, because it shows the writer choosing rather than simply being nice. The sudden silence in the third paragraph is an observation, not a statement of feeling, and observations score better. The last two lines contrast what she lost with what she gained in eleven words, which is the kind of ending a Primary 4 marker remembers.

oral2.title: Sleep and school start times
oral2.stimulus:
HEALTH PROMOTION BOARD · PUPIL SURVEY
How much sleep do we actually get?
Doctors recommend 9 to 11 hours a night for children aged 6 to 13. Pupils in the survey who slept fewer than 8 hours were twice as likely to report falling asleep in class. The most common reason given for a late bedtime was not homework but screens in the bedroom.

questions.q: What do you find most interesting about the information in this survey?
questions.model: The part I find most interesting is that the amount of sleep drops steadily as pupils get older, when you might expect the opposite, because older children have more homework but are also better at organising themselves. What struck me even more was the reason given at the bottom. I had assumed homework was the main cause of late bedtimes, so learning that screens in the bedroom mattered more than homework was surprising. It suggests the problem is not that children have too much to do, but that we find it very hard to stop once we have started watching something.

questions.q: Tell me about your own bedtime routine. Is it something you would change?
questions.model: On school nights I am supposed to be in bed by half past nine, and most of the time I am. What actually happens is that I lie there with my tablet for another twenty minutes, so I fall asleep closer to ten. I would change one thing: I would leave the tablet charging in the living room instead of on my bedside table. My mother suggested that months ago and I resisted, but looking at this survey I can see she was right. The nights I sleep best are the ones when I have left it outside, usually because I forgot it there.

questions.q: Some people say primary schools should start later in the morning. What do you think?
questions.model: I agree to a certain extent, though I do not think it would solve the problem on its own. Starting at eight instead of half past seven would certainly help pupils who travel a long way, because some of my classmates leave home before six. However, I suspect that many children would simply sleep later rather than sleep longer, since the real cause according to this survey is what happens at bedtime, not what happens in the morning. What I would suggest instead is a later start twice a week, perhaps on the two days with the heaviest lessons, together with a rule that phones and tablets are charged outside the bedroom. That way we would be tackling both ends of the night rather than just one.

oral2.title: Learning to cook at home
oral2.stimulus:
SCHOOL NEWSLETTER · HOME SKILLS
Can you cook one meal on your own?
In a survey of 480 Primary 4 to 6 pupils, 62% said they had never cooked anything using a stove. The most common thing pupils could prepare without help was instant noodles. Of the pupils who cooked regularly at home, almost all said they had learnt from a grandparent, not from a lesson or a video.

questions.q: What can you tell me about the information in this newsletter?
questions.model: The newsletter shows that most pupils in my level cannot cook very much. More than seven in ten can boil an egg, but fewer than two in ten can cook a vegetable dish, which needs cutting, heating oil and judging when something is done. I also noticed that nearly two thirds have never used a stove at all. The last sentence is the one I keep thinking about, though. The pupils who can cook learnt it from a grandparent rather than from a video, which tells me this is a skill that gets passed on by standing next to someone, not by watching a screen.

questions.q: Have you ever helped to prepare a meal? Tell me what happened.
questions.model: Yes, I have. Last year my mother taught me to make tomato and egg, which is the first dish she ever learnt herself. The first time, I put the eggs in before the pan was hot enough and they turned into a grey lump that stuck to the bottom. She made me scrub the pan and then let me try again the same evening, which I did not enjoy at the time. Now I can make it properly and I cook it on Saturdays when my parents are both working. My younger brother says it is better than my mother's, but he says that only when she is in the room.

questions.q: Do you think cooking should be taught in primary school? Why?
questions.model: I strongly believe it should, because cooking is one of the few subjects that every single person will use for the rest of their life, whatever job they end up doing. Knowing how to cook simple food also makes people healthier, since someone who can prepare a vegetable dish in fifteen minutes is far less likely to buy fried food every day. I know that schools worry about safety with stoves and knives, and that is a fair concern, so I would begin with dishes that need no heat at all in the lower primary levels, such as sandwiches and salads, and move on to the stove only in Primary 5 and 6 in small groups. Even a single term of lessons would mean that nobody leaves primary school able to cook only instant noodles.

oral2.title: Litter in the neighbourhood
oral2.stimulus:
TOWN COUNCIL · CLEANLINESS REPORT
Who actually picks it up?
Our town council employs 38 cleaners to sweep the estate every day. A one-week count found that 82% of the litter collected was dropped within ten metres of a bin. In a trial, painting bright footprints on the ground leading to the bins reduced litter in that block by a third, without any fines being issued.

questions.q: What do you think is the most important point in this report?
questions.model: For me the most important figure is that 82% of the litter was dropped within ten metres of a bin. That changes how I understand the problem completely. If the litter were far from any bin, the answer would be to build more bins, but it is not, so the issue is not convenience at all. People walk past a bin and drop something anyway. The footprint trial at the end supports that reading, because painting footprints does not make the bins any closer or any emptier. It only makes people notice them, and that alone cut the litter by a third without a single fine.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you saw someone drop litter. What did you do?
questions.model: A few months ago I was walking home from the market with my father when a man ahead of us finished a drink and left the plastic cup on top of an electrical box beside the lift lobby. There was a bin at the foot of the block, perhaps five steps away. I did not say anything to him, partly because I was nervous and partly because my father had already put his hand on my shoulder. After the man had gone into the lift, my father picked the cup up and threw it away, and he said one thing: that somebody always clears it, and it is never the person who left it. I have thought about that sentence many times since, and it is why I now pick things up on my own floor.

questions.q: What would you do to keep your neighbourhood clean, if it were up to you?
questions.model: I would spend the money on making bins impossible to ignore rather than on fines. The footprint trial in this report cut litter by a third for the price of some paint, which is remarkable, so I would paint footprints in every block and repaint them when they fade. Secondly, I would put a small bin at the entrance of every lift lobby, because that is where people finish their drinks while waiting. Thirdly, and this matters most to me, I would have primary school classes spend one morning a term clearing their own estate with the cleaners. It is easy to drop a cup when litter feels like somebody else's job, and much harder once you have spent a morning bending down to pick it up yourself. Fines punish the few people who are caught. Changing how the place feels changes everybody.

readAloud2.text: My father has kept the same wooden toolbox for twenty-three years. The handle is worn smooth, one hinge is held on with wire, and inside there is a jumble of screwdrivers, a hammer with a chipped head and a tin of nails that he refuses to throw away. Last month my mother bought him a new plastic toolbox for his birthday, with neat compartments and a lock. He thanked her warmly, admired it for a while, and then carried it into the store room. The old one is still by the door, where he can reach it.
notes: 'twenty-three' — keep both parts clear; do not swallow the 'three'.
The list in the second sentence has four items. Pause slightly at each comma so the list can be heard.
Final consonants: kept, worn, chipped, refuses, thanked, admired, carried.
Stress 'new' in the third sentence and 'old' in the last one — the contrast is the point of the passage.
The last sentence is the punchline. Slow down and let 'where he can reach it' land.

readAloud2.text: Hawker centres were not built for food. They were built for order. In the nineteen sixties, thousands of street hawkers cooked over open fires along the five-foot ways of Singapore, and the government wanted them licensed, plumbed and inspected. So it put up halls with concrete floors and numbered stalls, and moved everybody indoors. Nobody at the time imagined that these plain buildings would one day be listed by UNESCO, or that queues would form at seven in the morning for a bowl of noodles cooked by a man in his eighties who has never changed his recipe.
notes: Open with a firm, almost flat delivery on the first two sentences — they are a surprising claim and work best when stated plainly.
'nineteen sixties', 'five-foot ways', 'UNESCO' — say each of these slowly; they are the hard ones.
'licensed, plumbed and inspected' — three past participles in a row. Sound the final -ed on each.
Pause after 'So it put up halls with concrete floors and numbered stalls,' before 'and moved everybody indoors'.
Lift your voice on 'never changed his recipe' at the end — it carries the admiration.

readAloud2.text: The first person to swim across the Straits of Johor for charity did it in nineteen eighty-two, and she was fifty-six years old. She had learnt to swim at the age of forty-nine, in a public pool, from a teacher who charged her nothing. When reporters asked what the hardest part had been, they expected her to say the current, or the cold, or the jellyfish. She said it was the first morning at the pool, standing at the shallow end in a borrowed swimming costume while children half her height swam past her. Everything after that, she said, was merely water.
notes: Say 'nineteen eighty-two' and 'fifty-six' distinctly — the two numbers are the hook of the passage.
'the current, or the cold, or the jellyfish' — a list of three. Give each one equal weight and pause before the last.
The fourth sentence is long. Breathe after 'shallow end' and again after 'costume'.
Stress 'first morning' — it answers the reporters' question and overturns their expectation.
'was merely water' — drop your voice and slow right down. Do not rush the final three words.

readAloud2.text: Consider the humble queue. It is one of the few things in public life that works entirely on agreement: there is no law compelling you to stand behind the person who arrived before you, and yet almost everybody does. Watch what happens when somebody steps in near the front. Nobody shouts. Instead there is a ripple of glances, a shifting of bags, a pointed clearing of the throat, and very often the offender retreats without a word being spoken to them. It is a remarkably efficient system, held together by nothing more solid than the fear of being looked at.
notes: Open conversationally on 'Consider the humble queue' — you are inviting the listener to notice something.
'compelling', 'offender', 'remarkably', 'efficient' — practise these four aloud before you begin.
The list in the fourth sentence builds: glances, bags, throat. Let each one get slightly more emphasis.
Pause after 'Nobody shouts.' It is a short sentence on purpose, and the pause does the work.
Land firmly on 'the fear of being looked at' — this is the joke and the point at the same time.
